problems.source_says: The text gives two names for this Task 2 score. Section 2.3 defines rating (1) as 'creativity (i.e., the novel and useful level of idea)', and Table 2b heads the column 'Creativity'. But the paper's test table and figure call it novelty: Table 1 Task2-Variable 'novelty' (Day 2: -0.99, -4.05, 0.000) equals the Table 2b gap (2.83 - 3.82), and Figure 2b labels the panel 'Novelty'. Table 1 and Figure 2b also carry a separate Task 2 'usefulness' score, and p. 7 says Figures 2a and 2b show the parts 'related to novelty and usefulness' for both tasks. This fits a creativity rating split into novelty and usefulness sub-scores, as in the AUT. Under that reading the construct is novelty. The text cannot settle it, and the form does not list it as an open question. The choice matters: codebook section 8 ranks overall creativity first for the with_ai primary record, so S1-O2 coded overall_creativity would become primary over AUT novelty. Fix: add an open question and do not let the primary-record choice rest on this label; or code novelty, following the label of the analysis (Table 1, Figure 2b).

problems.source_says: The paper never describes a Task 2 usefulness rating. Section 2.3 lists four Task 2 ratings (creativity, content quality, public popularity, market success), and Table 2b has no usefulness column. The form's coding is an inference from the fact that the only Task 2 raters were the two with new-project-development experience. The form says so in measure_detail ('how this rating was made is not described'). The coding has text support only under the reading in which 'creativity (i.e., the novel and useful level of idea)' was rated as separate novelty and usefulness scores. That reading makes S1-O2 a novelty score, not overall creativity. So the form's codes for S1-O2 and S1-O5 rest on two different readings of the same sentence. Fix: code both outcomes from one reading, and keep the open question on how Task 2 usefulness was scored.
problems.quote: another two raters who had rich work experiences on new project development were instructed to independently rate participants’ responses in four different ways: (1) creativity (i.e., the novel and useful level of idea)
problems.locator: p. 6, Section 2.3; p. 8, Table 2b; pp. 11-12, Table 1; p. 10, Figure 2b

problems.source_says: The Day 7 AUT values show the same split that the form codes 'mixed' for S1-O15 (Task 2, Day 7) and S1-O8. SBERT similarity (0.33 vs 0.36) and string matching (2.76 vs 3.74) are higher for GPT (less diverse). Table 4a standard deviation (0.37 vs 0.38) and sum of eigenvalues (0.14 vs 0.15) are also higher for GPT (more dispersed), and ellipse area is equal (0.22 vs 0.22). No Day 7 test is reported. The text's claim that lower dispersion 'was continuing at Day 7 and Day 30' (p. 17) fails at Day 7 on standard deviation and sum of eigenvalues in both Table 4a and Table 4b. This is outside checks (a) to (e), but it is a coding inconsistency. Fix: code this contrast 'mixed', as for S1-O15, or 'no_clear_difference' (no test, a 0.03 gap); or recode S1-O8 and S1-O15 under one rule.

confirmed.statement: No outcome is self-reported. All are scored on participants' output: two blind raters per task (consensual assessment technique, ICCs ≥ .90) rated each AUT idea for novelty and usefulness and each Task 2 response; flexibility counts each participant's unique usage categories; SBERT and string matching are computed on the answer texts.
confirmed.locator: p. 6, Section 2.3; p. 13, Section 3.2; p. 15, string matching

confirmed.statement: AI availability is coded correctly. The treatment group had ChatGPT 4.0 on Days 2 to 6. All participants worked without it on Day 1 and Day 7, and the Day 30 AUT was done without ChatGPT. So ai_available_when_produced is 'yes' for S1-O1 to S1-O8 and 'no' for S1-O9 to S1-O15.
confirmed.locator: p. 5, Section 2.2, second and third paragraphs; p. 5, Figure 1; p. 14, Section 3.2; p. 22, Discussion

confirmed.statement: The question codes follow the codebook rule for all 15 outcomes: rated outcomes produced with AI are with_ai (S1-O1 to S1-O6), similarity with AI is across_people (S1-O7, S1-O8), and every Day 7 or Day 30 outcome is after_ai (S1-O9 to S1-O15), diversity included.
confirmed.locator: codebook section 1; form-spec field note on 'question'

confirmed.statement: Unit 'participant' is right for the rated outcomes. Novelty and usefulness are participant sums of idea scores, groups are compared by t-tests, and the Table 1 note says N=61. The printed t and P pairs fit about 59 degrees of freedom (t = -2.21, P 0.031; t = -2.12, P 0.038; t = -2.37, P 0.021), which is a participant-level test.
confirmed.locator: p. 6, Section 2.3; p. 7, Section 3.1, last paragraph; pp. 11-12, Table 1 and note

confirmed.statement: Flexibility (S1-O4, S1-O12) is variety within one participant's own ideas ('Flexibility of each participant ... counting the total number of unique usage categories'), so construct 'flexibility' and measure 'category_count' fit.

The diversity outcomes compare different people. Task 2 has 427 solutions from 61 participants over 7 days (61 x 7 = 427, one solution per participant per day), so every Task 2 pair compares two people. The paper frames AUT similarity as convergence 'at a group level'. Whether two ideas from the same participant are paired is not stated, as computed_over records.
confirmed.locator: p. 1, abstract; p. 5, Section 2.3; p. 13, Section 3.2; p. 22, Discussion

confirmed.statement: Unit 'pair' for the SBERT outcomes is the paper's computation: cosine similarity between two answers, reported as group means (M_C, M_E). The test behind 'ps ≤ .01' and 'p ≤ .001' is not named, as diversity_detail records.

Content quality ('the writing, structures, and logics of the idea') coded as 'usefulness' fits the codebook definition ('quality of a single output'). Task 2 raters had 'rich work experiences on new project development', so 'expert_raters' holds for S1-O2, S1-O6, and S1-O10. The AUT raters' background is not stated, and 'human_raters' is the remaining code for them.

Every number in the 15 'reported' fields matches the PDF. This covers the Table 2a and 2b means (bolding included), the Table 1 Estimate, Statistic, and P Value rows, the P labels in Figure 2a, Figure 2b, and appendix Figure 2b, the Table 3 SBERT and string-matching values, the Table 4a and 4b standard deviation, eigenvalue, and ellipse values, and the text ranges on pp. 14-15.

Table 1 Estimate equals Control minus GPT: 30.77 - 41.55 = -10.78 (AUT novelty, Day 2), 27.27 - 26.73 = 0.54 (AUT usefulness, Day 7), 3.38 - 3.90 = -0.52 (Task 2, Day 7). As the form records, the Day 30 estimates (-3.69, -6.26) do not equal the Table 2a gaps (-0.16, 0.07).

The conflicts the form records are in the PDF: Day 30 AUT novelty has P 0.038 in Table 1, but the text reports no significant difference; Day 7 Task 2 usefulness has P 0.021, but the text says 'all p-values were insignificant'; Table 4b has larger standard deviations and eigenvalue sums for GPT, against the claim on p. 17.

summary: All 15 outcomes are scored on participants' output, the AI-availability, question, timing, and unit codes are supported by the text, and every reported number matches the PDF tables and figures (pp. 8-17, 28-30). The coding is still refuted: the Task 2 score coded overall_creativity (S1-O2, S1-O10) is labeled 'novelty' in the paper's test table and figure beside a Task 2 'usefulness' score that Section 2.3 never describes, so S1-O2 and S1-O5/S1-O13 rest on two conflicting readings of one sentence, and the Day 7 AUT similarity contrast (S1-O14) is coded treatment_lower although it shows the same split that the form codes 'mixed' for S1-O15.
